query: For multiprincipal-element alloys intended for sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs oxidation resistance and material integrity, and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, relevant supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC-based multiprincipal-element alloys (MPEAs) with Ni–Co–Fe as the primary matrix, oxidation resistance and long-term material integrity at 900–1100°C are governed by whether Al/Cr-rich regions percolate through the matrix and grain-boundary network to sustain a continuous, adherent external Al2O3/Cr2O3 scale. This percolation is mediated by short-range order (SRO) and segregation that raise the effective activity of Al/Cr at the surface relative to internal sinks. When Al+Cr are below a percolation threshold or disrupted by fine grains/high boundary area, oxidation proceeds via mixed, non-protective spinels and internal oxidation, degrading integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: FCC Ni–Co–Fe–(Al,Cr) MPEAs with identical total Ni+Co+Fe content and equiatomic balance among these three elements; two baseline variants: (i) low Al+Cr combined (~15 at%) with fine grains (~10–20 µm), solutionized and water quenched; (ii) high Al+Cr combined (~28 at%) with coarse grains (~200–500 µm), solutionized then annealed to induce SRO and slow-cooled to retain it. No reactive elements in the baseline.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary (a) Al+Cr combined content across a threshold (e.g., ~15 at% vs ~28 at%) at fixed Ni–Co–Fe, (b) grain size (fine vs coarse via high-T anneal), and (c) add trace reactive element (0.05–0.2 at% Y) in matched pairs. Use a 2×2×2 factorial to isolate composition, microstructure, and reactive-element effects while keeping total valence electron concentration and phase (FCC) constant.
generation.conditions: Dry air (pO2 ~0.21 atm), 900–1100°C, isothermal exposures for 100–500 h and cyclic thermal shocks between 200°C and test temperature every 12 h; low water vapor (<0.1% H2O) to minimize volatilization effects; specimens mechanically polished, edges sealed to avoid geometric artifacts.
generation.structural_mediator: Al/Cr short-range order and grain-boundary segregation that create a percolating Al/Cr-rich network accessible to the surface, plus reduced grain-boundary area in coarse-grained states limiting oxygen ingress. Reactive-element (Y) occupancy at oxide/metal interface suppresses cation-vacancy flux and improves scale adherence.
generation.mechanism: Selective external oxidation is favored when the effective chemical activity and transport of Al/Cr to the surface exceed oxygen ingress and internal sink capture: (i) SRO raises local Al/Cr activity and reduces their dissolution into mixed spinels; (ii) a percolating Al/Cr network sustains outward cation flux to form continuous Al2O3/Cr2O3; (iii) coarse grains limit fast oxygen transport along boundaries, suppressing internal oxidation; (iv) Y reduces void formation and interfacial stresses, decreasing spallation. When Al+Cr are below threshold or disrupted by high boundary density, oxygen penetrates along boundaries and forms non-protective mixed oxides (Ni/Co/Fe spinels), leading to internal oxidation and decohesion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the low-Al+Cr, fine-grained baseline without Y: (1) High-Al+Cr, coarse-grained variants will exhibit predominantly continuous Al2O3 or Cr2O3 at the surface, parabolic oxidation kinetics with an at least several-fold lower rate constant, shallow or negligible internal oxidation depth, and minimal spallation under cycling. (2) Adding trace Y to high-Al+Cr variants further reduces cyclic mass loss and increases scale adherence without substantially changing isothermal parabolic rate (directional improvement expected). (3) Low-Al+Cr fine-grained variants will show mixed spinel scales (Ni/Co/Fe oxides), near-linear-to-paralinear mass gain early on, deeper internal oxidation fronts (>tens of micrometers over 100–500 h), and pronounced spallation on thermal cycling. Magnitude expectations are directional: high-Al+Cr+coarse+Y should have notably lower mass gain and damage than baseline (order-of-magnitude reduction is plausible but not asserted here without supporting data).
generation.baseline: Low Al+Cr (~15 at%) FCC Ni–Co–Fe MPEA, fine-grained (~10–20 µm), no reactive element, solutionized and quenched: expected to form discontinuous, mixed spinel scales with internal oxidation and degraded integrity under 900–1100°C air.
generation.boundary: Hypothesis is expected to hold for FCC Ni–Co–Fe-(Al,Cr) MPEAs without high fractions of volatile or pesting oxide formers (e.g., Mo, V at significant levels), in dry air at 900–1100°C for up to 500 h isothermal or moderate thermal cycling. It may not hold if: (i) temperature exceeds ~1150–1200°C causing phase changes or rapid cation diffusion that disrupts protectiveness; (ii) high water vapor or sulfur/chlorine contaminants alter scale chemistry; (iii) very high Mn or other spinel formers skew selective oxidation; (iv) the alloy is BCC or contains significant ordered intermetallics altering diffusion pathways.
generation.uncertainty: Exact Al+Cr percolation threshold and the strength of SRO in these specific MPEAs are composition- and thermal-history dependent; the role of Cr vs Al can shift with temperature and environment; quantitative reductions in parabolic rate constants and spallation resistance are uncertain without data; reactive-element benefits depend on achieving appropriate interfacial coverage and may vary with Y content.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare four core compositions with identical Ni–Co–Fe totals: two with Al+Cr ~15 at% and ~28 at% (Al:Cr ratio held constant), each in fine (~10–20 µm) and coarse (~200–500 µm) grain states; duplicate each with and without 0.1 at% Y. Confirm single-phase FCC by XRD and composition uniformity by EPMA. Characterize SRO/percolation via APT or diffuse scattering where feasible. Expose all in identical dry air at 1000°C for 300 h (isothermal) and then subject to 20 thermal cycles (200↔1000°C). Measure oxidation kinetics by thermogravimetric analysis (in-situ for isothermal), post-exposure oxide chemistry and continuity by SEM/EDS and XPS, internal oxidation depth by cross-sectional TEM, grain-boundary oxidation by EBSD-assisted correlative microscopy, and scale adhesion via acoustic emission or four-point bend spallation test. Assess mechanical integrity via room-temperature tensile tests and elevated-temperature microhardness before and after exposure.
measurements: Mass gain vs time (derive parabolic rate constant where applicable)
Oxide scale phase identification and continuity (XRD, Raman, XPS, TEM)
Internal oxidation depth and grain-boundary penetration (cross-sectional TEM/SEM)
Scale adhesion/spallation (cyclic mass loss, acoustic emission events)
Elemental segregation/SRO indicators (APT or STEM-EDS mapping of Al/Cr at boundaries)
Post-exposure ductility and strength retention (tensile elongation, yield strength)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if either: (a) alloys with high Al+Cr and coarse grains (with or without Y) fail to form continuous Al2O3/Cr2O3 and instead exhibit oxidation kinetics and internal oxidation comparable to or worse than the low-Al+Cr fine-grained baseline; or (b) low-Al+Cr fine-grained alloys consistently form continuous protective Al2O3/Cr2O3 scales with low mass gain and minimal internal oxidation across the test window; or (c) measured Al/Cr SRO/percolation indicators do not correlate with protectiveness (i.e., samples with strong Al/Cr percolation still show non-protective behavior, while samples without percolation show protective scales).
